speaker: joshuathompson
text: Thank you. May it please the court, counsel. In this case, the trial court committed structural error when it denied T.M. his rights to a fair trial and due process. Specifically, the trial court favored the state by forming a fixed anticipatory judgment that T.M. should be adjudicated of felonious assault. It showed through its statements that it did not maintain an open state of mind in reaching its conclusion. Here, the procedural history of this case is important. This case was previously before this court and reversed because the trial court refused to grant T.M. a continuance to obtain the testimony of his witnesses. In the initial trial then, it adjudicated T.M. without the benefit of his witnesses. On remand, the trial was essentially reopened at the point that T.M.'s witnesses would testify. Therefore, the bias from the initial trial date in September 2018 is still relevant to the overall bias as well. There were four particular incidents indicating the trial court reached a fixed anticipatory judgment. First, when Angela West testified on cross-examination, defense counsel challenged her testimony with her recorded statement to police. The trial court said regarding the video, why are we watching this? What is the point you're trying to make? Can you get to it? This indicates a lack of interest in defense counsel's points on cross-examination, much like it had no interest in hearing from defense witnesses the first time around. Second, when T.M. testified, he said that Mr. Schmidt punched him first. He described the punch as a sucker punch. The trial court interjected without objection from the state and said, that's a mischaracterization. It was just punching. Let's clear that up or rephrase the question. And while a trial court can choose to believe or not believe testimony, there was nothing objectionable about T.M.'s statement that he was sucker punched. It was his personal opinion about the nature of the punch. To deny T.M. the ability to testify to his own perception of the incident is further proof that the trial court had reached a fixed anticipatory judgment. Third, when Jasmine testified on direct, defense counsel, having obviously observed Jasmine gesturing to show how Mr. Schmidt reached for T.M.'s legs, started to ask a question, defense counsel started to ask a question based on the gesture. The trial court interjected again without objection. I didn't see that. That's not accurate. You were leading the witness. Go ahead. Defense county counsel has a duty to present the truth in court. The trial court made a record that there was no gesturing made by the witness. In doing so, trial court essentially made a record that defense counsel presented a falsehood to the court. This showed favoritism to the state, a further indication that the trial court had reached a fixed anticipatory judgment. Finally, when Jasmine testified about how close Mr. Schmidt initially was to T.M., she first said four feet. When redirected by defense counsel, she corrected herself to two feet. Rather than simply reach its own conclusion about the distance, the trial court again spoke up, stating, I think it's a little bit further, two to four feet. That may seem on its face like the court making its own determination, but what's happening there is the trial court is indicating that the witness and defense theory was not to be believed, again showing favoritism toward the state. Moving to the second assignment of error, regardless of what this court reaches about the trial court's bias, the fact remains that T.M. should not have been adjudicated of felonious assault because his adjudication was based on insufficient evidence and was against the manifest weight of the evidence. It should first be noted that the trial court reached the contradictory conclusion that T.M. and Mr. Schmidt both squared up and engaged in a mutual fight, but that T.M. was guilty of felonious assault. A mutual fight is disorderly conduct under RC-29-17-11-A1. It does not become a felonious assault simply because one party accidentally suffered a serious injury. Second, the trial court erred in relying solely on the foreseeability of injury from the incident. Much like the reasonable doubt standard where every incident is subject to some imaginary doubt, any possible outcome of a fight could theoretically be foreseen. The question here, however, under the definition of knowingly in RC-29-03-11-A1 is whether T.M. was aware that his conduct would probably cause a certain result or probably be of a certain nature. In other words, was T.M. aware that his conduct would probably lead to Mr. Schmidt suffering a traumatic brain injury? Here, there is no evidence to indicate that T.M. knowingly caused the serious physical harm Mr. Schmidt suffered. Even if the state were to show recklessness on T.M.'s behalf doing so would be insufficient to prove knowledge. A reckless cause of serious physical harm would be an assault, not a felonious assault. For example, in State v. Berry, 2007, Ohio, 7082, from the 12th District, the court found that although the defendant knowingly slammed a glass to the floor, which would cause a glass to break, it could not conclude that the defendant was subjectively aware his actions would harm his nearby wife. Furthermore, in State v. Hancock, 2004, Ohio, 1492, this court found that a couple struggling over a phone, which led to the phone striking the alleged victim was insufficient to establish knowledge of the harm. The events here are undoubtedly fortunate and unfortunate and sad, but they did not establish knowledge. We essentially were presented with five viewpoints on what happened. Mr. Schmidt was unable to testify about how he fell to the ground. He could only guess. Angela West changed her testimony from her statement to police. She initially confirmed that Mr. Schmidt tried to grab TM. TM grabbed Mr. Schmidt back and they both went down with TM falling on his back and Mr. Schmidt falling on top of TM. At trial, she claimed TM grabbed Mr. Schmidt from behind and fell back, causing them both to fall. TM testified that Mr. Schmidt punched him first and then TM punched him back. Mr. Schmidt grabbed TM's shirt, TM grabbed his shoulders, both fell and then TM ran away. Alexis and Jasmine, who were allowed to testify on remand, both confirmed that Mr. Schmidt punched first. They said Mr. Schmidt went for TM's legs and TM put Mr. Schmidt in a bear hug and again, both fell. Until Angela Schmidt or Angela West changed her testimony during trial, everyone who could testify about the fall agreed that TM fell on his back and Mr. Schmidt fell on him. The evidence clearly shows that TM did not knowingly cause serious physical harm to Mr. Schmidt. Even if this court concludes that TM acted knowingly, the weight of the evidence shows that TM acted in self-defense. Even the court concluded that TM and Mr. Schmidt squared up to fight. The evidence presented at trial shows Mr. Schmidt swung on TM first. Looking to the elements of self-defense, TM was not at fault in creating the situation, giving rise to the afraid. Specifically, Mr. Schmidt initiated the verbal confrontation and he swung first. For the same reason that Mr. Schmidt swung first, TM certainly had reasonable grounds to believe he was in imminent danger of bodily harm. Regardless of TM's size, Mr. Schmidt was an adult man and although unknown to TM, Mr. Schmidt had a military background. Finally, regarding the amount of force used, all TM did was grab Mr. Schmidt. The fall was accidental and the severity of the injuries was incidental and a freak accident. The state did not disprove TM acted in self-defense. The bottom line here is that the evidence showed that TM was approached by an adult, verbally accosted by him and then punched by him. As he was allowed to do, TM returned the punch. When Mr. Schmidt grabbed him, TM grabbed him back. Now, unfortunately, they both fell and Mr. Schmidt suffered serious injuries. But TM did not knowingly cause serious physical harm to Mr. Schmidt. His actions were not reckless and the actions he did take were justified by self-defense. He was adjudicated by a court that had reached a fixed anticipatory judgment in favor of the state. For those reasons, we ask that this court reverse and vacate TM's adjudication.
